did_you_know.text: The cubit was an ancient unit of length, but its exact size was not always the same. So the altar’s dimensions are approximate rather than precise modern measurements.
The word “horns” literally means horns, and these were projections at the altar’s four corners. Similar altar projections are known from the ancient Near East.
The women’s mirrors were made of polished metal, since glass mirrors like the ones we use today were not common in that period.
From the measurements in verses 9–13, the courtyard can be understood as a rectangle: one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide. It formed an open space around the Tabernacle.
The entrance screen used the same main colors mentioned for the priestly garments and the Tabernacle’s curtains. The entrance was therefore not merely functional but also part of the sacred design.
This is one of the Torah’s early descriptions of an organized record of public property. Ithamar, Aaron’s son, was placed in charge of the Levites’ work and its supervision.

Bezalel belonged to the tribe of Judah and Oholiab to the tribe of Dan, so the Tabernacle is presented as a shared project of people from different tribes. Bezalel led the work, while Oholiab was a skilled craftsman.
A “talent” was a large unit of metal weight, not a particular coin. Since its exact weight varied across periods, the amount cannot be converted into a certain number of modern kilograms.

Everyone counted from the age of twenty and up gave half a shekel, so the contribution did not depend on a person’s wealth. The number in the verse indicates a census of more than six hundred thousand people.
One hundred talents of silver were cast into one hundred bases, so each base received one talent. These heavy bases helped support the posts of the Tabernacle and the curtain.
